titre: Eunice Foote, 1856: Carbon Dioxide Heats Up in the Sun
accroche: In 1856, a cylinder of carbon dioxide heats up more in the sun than a cylinder of air. The result is read in Albany by Joseph Henry, not by its author.
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 1856, in Albany, New York, the 10th annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science hears a paper on the heat of the sun. Its author does not read it. Joseph Henry, of the Smithsonian Institution, does so in her place, stating in a preface that science has neither country nor sex.

The author is Eunice Foote, probably the wife of Elisha Foote, of Seneca Falls: Wells does not give her affiliation; that is Sorenson's deduction. The account given by David Wells in his *Annual of Scientific Discovery* describes a simple protocol.

## Cylinders in the Sun

Two glass cylinders, each fitted with a thermometer, are brought to the same temperature and then placed side by side in the sun. In one, Foote compresses the air; in the other, she rarefies it. The thermometer in the compressed air rises more than twenty degrees above the other. She then compares air saturated with moisture and air dried with calcium chloride: a difference of about twelve degrees.

Then she fills one cylinder with carbon dioxide and the other with ordinary air. The first heats up distinctly more, by about twenty degrees, and takes longer to cool. The account draws a consequence from this: an atmosphere of this gas would give the Earth a much higher temperature, and if the air had contained more of it in the past, it would have been warmer then.

## Seeing an Effect, Measuring It

Three years later, in 1859, John Tyndall presents to the Royal Society his first results on the passage of radiant heat through gases, and says he knows of no published experiment on the subject. In 1861, he gives quantified measurements: carbon dioxide, water vapor, and hydrocarbons absorb radiant heat far more than oxygen and nitrogen, which make up most of the air.

The difference lies in the question asked. Foote records an overall heating in a cylinder exposed to the sun; she does not say what share of the heat received the gas itself retains. Tyndall isolates that absorption, gas by gas, and puts a number on it. This reading of the gap between the two protocols is ours, not that of the sources.

## What History Remembers

In the usual account, everything starts with Tyndall. Yet her work had been in print: summarized in 1857 in Wells's annual, and, according to The Public Domain Review, published in full in the *American Journal of Science* (2nd series, vol. XXII, pp. 382-383). It is an independent geologist, Raymond Sorenson, who republishes Wells's account in 2011 to restore its place; he believed Foote's text had never been published in proper form, which the previous source contradicts.

Foote's result is therefore not a hidden discovery: it remained little cited. How many other observations are waiting in pages that no one reopens?

repere.texte: In Wells's account (1857), compressed air heats up more than twenty degrees more than rarefied air, humid air about twelve degrees more than dried air, and carbon dioxide about twenty degrees more than ordinary air.
repere.source: Raymond Sorenson, “Eunice Foote's Pioneering Research On CO2 And Climate Warming,” AAPG Search and Discovery, 2011 (reproducing Wells, Annual of Scientific Discovery, 1857, pp. 159-160)

carte.punch: In 1856, a woman shows that CO₂ heats up in the sun. A man reads her paper.
carte.idee: In 1856, Joseph Henry reads Eunice Foote's paper in Albany: a cylinder of carbon dioxide heats up about twenty degrees more than a cylinder of air. Tyndall will quantify the absorption gas by gas in 1861.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Tyndall's work (1859-1861) from Foote's experiment (1856)?
choix: Tyndall studies the Sun, Foote only artificial heat sources
Tyndall publishes before Foote, who is merely repeating his results
Tyndall measures the absorption of radiant heat gas by gas, with quantified values
Tyndall works on air alone, Foote on carbon dioxide alone
quiz.explication: Foote records an overall heating of cylinders exposed to the sun, in 1856. Tyndall, starting in 1859, isolates the absorption of radiant heat by each gas and quantifies it in 1861. He therefore does not publish before her, and both do work on several gases.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who reads Foote's paper at the AAAS meeting in Albany in 1856?
choix: Joseph Henry, of the Smithsonian Institution
John Tyndall, visiting the United States
Her husband Elisha Foote, a judge and inventor
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wells's account specifies that Joseph Henry reads the text in her place. The account names neither Tyndall, who was then working in England, nor Elisha Foote as the reader.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In Wells's account, by how much more does the carbon dioxide cylinder heat up than the ordinary air cylinder?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Carbon dioxide rises about twenty degrees more than ordinary air. The twelve degrees concern a different comparison: humid air versus air dried with calcium chloride.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What consequence does the account draw from the heating of the carbon dioxide cylinder?
choix: An atmosphere of this gas would make the Earth much warmer
An atmosphere of this gas would cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight
This gas plays no role outside the laboratory
This gas heats the air but never the surface of the ground
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The account concludes that an atmosphere of carbon dioxide would give the Earth a much higher temperature, and that it would have been warmer in the past if the air had contained more of it.
